title: Bhutan, end to end
standfirst: A country that limits its own visitors, which is exactly why it repays the time.

blocks.heading: West to east, if there is time
paras: Almost every Bhutan itinerary covers Paro, Thimphu and Punakha and stops. Those three valleys are lovely and they are also where everyone else is.
East of Trongsa the country changes: fewer visitors, older weaving traditions, longer drives. A member with twelve nights can reach it by road and fly back from the east.

blocks.heading: Festivals set the calendar
blocks.caption: Valley festivals fix the dates; the rest follows.
paras: The tsechu festivals move with the lunar calendar and fill the good rooms in a valley within days of being announced.
We check festival dates before anything else, then build the route around them rather than hoping to catch one in passing.

blocks.heading: Walking, not trekking
blocks.caption: Short daily walks rather than one long effort.
paras: The climb to Taktsang is the famous one and it is genuinely steep. Everything else can be as gentle as a member wants.
We prefer a short walk every day to one heroic day, which keeps the legs willing and leaves the afternoons free.

blocks.heading: Questions members ask
blocks.intro: The ones that come up nearly every time.

a: March to May and September to November. The valleys are clearest either side of the monsoon, and those windows carry most of the festivals.
Bhutan sets a daily levy per visitor in addition to the cost of travel, which is deliberate policy rather than a markup. It is the reason the valleys are not crowded.
Seven nights for the western valleys. Twelve or more if you want to cross to the east, which we would encourage if the time exists.

blocks.heading: We are ready when you are
paras: Every itinerary starts with a conversation about what you actually want from the days, and works backwards to houses, guides and timing from there.
